input.question: How do we actually know the age of the Earth? (Repost)
input.ground_truth: Elements like uranium and thorium are unstable and they decay into elements which are not stable themselves and so on. This is called a radioactive cascade or decay chain. Since these elements existed prior to the formation of the solar system, we can determine the ratios of the end products and knowing the decay rates of the decay chain, calculate how long ago the rock was formed. When we do this what we measure is *not* the age of the elements but of the rock itself because when rock is formed, most of the final elements of the decay chain can escape and the radiodating process is 'reset'.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How do we actually know the age of the Earth? (Repost)

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you want to know how old your big, big birthday cake is. You can’t just look at it and guess. But you can look at the candles that have been put on it before, or maybe see how many layers the cake has, and how long it takes to bake each layer.

Scientists want to know how old the Earth is, just like you want to know how old your cake is. They can’t just count the years, because there were no people to count them a long, long time ago.

So, scientists use special clues. One clue is rocks! The Earth is made of rocks, and some rocks are really, really old. Inside these rocks, there are tiny things called crystals that form over time, like layers in your cake.

Another clue is something called “meteorites.” These are rocks from space that fell to Earth a long time ago. Scientists think these rocks are about the same age as the Earth, like if your cake and a space cake were baked at the same time!

By studying these rocks and using math and special clocks that can tell how old things are (called “radiometric dating”), scientists can figure out that the Earth is about 4 and a half billion years old. That’s like 4,500,000,000 years! That’s a lot of birthdays!
